brief_context: Jurisdiction of the Electricity Commission for supply supervision.
brief_extract:
The First Serious Attempt
The Electricity (Supply) Act, 1919, was the first serious attempt to organise the Electricity Supply Industry on a national basis, and was the result of the “Williamson” Committee. Provision was made for the establishment of the Electricity Commission, responsible to the Minister of Transport for promotion, generation and supervision of the supply of electricity in the United Kingdom. In Parliament the responsibility for electricity supply then passed from the Board of Trade to the Ministry of Transport, and now rests with the Ministry of Fuel and Power.

brief_context: Country with a completely interconnected high voltage transmission system.
brief_extract: The Central Electricity Board was created for the purpose of co-ordinating the production of electricity on a national basis; concentrating generation in a limited number of “selected” stations; providing the Grid to inter-connect these stations; affording bulk supplies; and standardising frequency. Great Britain is the only country with a completely interconnected high voltage transmission system. Further powers were conferred in 1935 and 1936 and, the generation side of the Industry having been put on a satisfactory footing, Sir John Snell, who had been so prominent in this respect, devoted the greater part of his last years to the reorganisation of distribution.

Walsall, Wolverhampton and Ocker Hill, and the great new station at Ironbridge, are interconnected and linked to the Grid. JANUARY, 1947

Impressions of U.S.A. and Canada

By VERA NORVICK

TO go out by small freighter and return home by the Aquitania, still a troopship, was a fitting framework of contrast for a visit to the U.S.A. and Canada, where it was continually necessary to adjust one's mental perspective.

brief_context: Region described as reminiscent of the author's home country.
brief_extract: and Canada, where it was continually necessary to adjust one's mental perspective. The New England countryside was an extended recollection of this country. brief_context: Location of the proposed Severn Barrage tidal power scheme.
brief_extract: It is not intended in this article to deal with all forms of water power, but only with tidal power schemes. The Severn Barrage Scheme was one proposal for using tidal power, and has been the subject of two official reports, one in 1933, and the other in 1945. Experts agree that both on economic and technical grounds it is sound and would save about 1 1/2 million tons of coal per year.

brief_context: Mentioned in the context of the Severn Barrage Scheme.
brief_extract: The objection to tidal power stations is that they only generate electricity at certain states of the tide. The Severn Barrage Scheme, for instance, would generate elec- tricity during two periods of seven hours in every 24. They may give rise to occasional small tech- nical difficulties on the Grid Network, because the times of generation would not necessarily coincide with peak consumer demand, but this would become less as the national load increased.

brief_context: Site of the proposed tidal power scheme.
brief_extract:
Overcoming Difficulties
Pumped storage would over- come this disadvantage but at an increased cost of the resultant energy, also the establishment of a series of tidal power stations all supplying the grid, would tend, in the aggregate, to give a con- tinuous supply because the times of the tides are different at different places. A Tidal Power Scheme, now under consideration by the Ministry of Fuel and Power, which overcomes the above dis- advantage of intermittent out- put, is the Menai Straits Tidal Power Scheme, proposed by the writer, and incorporates a storage system at little additional cost and negligible loss in efficiency. The Menai Straits are open to the sea at both ends, and by con- structing three dams, they can be divided into two reservoirs of approximately equal water surface area.

brief_context: Location of one of the dams in the scheme.
brief_extract:
The Menai Straits are open to the sea at both ends, and by con- structing three dams, they can be divided into two reservoirs of approximately equal water surface area. The reservoir at the Bangor end will be kept at the highest possible level, by topping
up at each high tide at the Bangor dam. The other, at the Caernarvon end, will be kept at the lowest possible level, by draining to the sea at each low tide, at the opposite end of the Straits.

brief_context: Location of one of the dams in the scheme.
brief_extract:
The reservoir at the Bangor end will be kept at the highest possible level, by topping
up at each high tide at the Bangor dam. The other, at the Caernarvon end, will be kept at the lowest possible level, by draining to the sea at each low tide, at the opposite end of the Straits. The Bangor dam sluices will only allow the sea to enter into the high level reservoir, they will always keep the water in when the sea level is lower.

brief_context: Location of the dam sluices in the Straits.
brief_extract: The Bangor dam sluices will only allow the sea to enter into the high level reservoir, they will always keep the water in when the sea level is lower. The Belan dam sluices at the other end of the Straits will keep the sea out and allow the low level reservoir to empty into the sea at low tide. By this means, there will always be a substantial difference in water level between the two reser- voirs, that is, at the centre dam.

NORTH OF SCOTLAND
WATER POWER SCHEMES
The Hydro-Electric Development (Scotland) Act, 1943, established the North of Scotland Hydro-Electric Board, which has made steady progress in bringing electricity supply from water power to the most isolated parts of the Highlands and Islands of Scotland. In connection with the latest project, that of Mullardoch-Fasnakyle-Affric, the contract has been put in hand for three 22,000 kW turbo alternators for the Fasnakyle generating station; arrangements are completed for the erection of camps to house the peak number of 2,000 men to build the dams and power stations and drive the necessary tunnels.

The purpose of the Bill is to provide for the co-ordination under public ownership of the Electricity Supply Industry, and the policy suggested will be:—
(a) the economical generation, transmission and distribution of electricity
(b) the cheapening of supply so far as practicable
(c) the avoidance of undue preference in provision of supply
(d) simplification of tariffs
(e) standardisation of systems of supply and of electrical fittings
(f) securing the welfare, health and safety, training and education of employees
(g) facilitating research, and specifically research in district heating. The Bill proposes the establishment of:—
(1) A British Electricity Authority (Central Authority)
(2) 14 Area Boards
(3) The North of Scotland Board
(4) A Consultative Council in the area of each Board. In general the work of (1) and (2) is the responsibility of the Minister of Fuel and Power, and (3) of the Secretary of State for Scotland.

“The Electrical Age” joins with the whole electricity supply industry in congratulating Sir John Kennedy, O.B.E., M.Inst.C.E., on his Honorary Membership of the Institution of Electrical Engineers, and Sir Leonard Pearce, C.B.E., D.Sc., on the award of the Faraday Medal “for his outstanding contributions to the advancement of engineering practice and notable achievements in electrical engineering.” Sir John Kennedy, now Deputy Chairman of the Electricity Commission, prepared for the Electricity Commissioners the technical and financial data upon which are based the regional schemes resulting from the creation of the “Grid” by the Electricity Supply Act of 1926. Sir Leonard Pearce is the Engineer-in-Chief of the London Power Company, and was responsible for the engineering design of the Battersea Power Station. Sir Leonard’s honour coincides with the 21st Anniversary of the London Power Company celebrated in February.

OCTOBER, 1947

Help from a Canadian Kitchen

By SOPHIE MATHESON, a member of the E.A.W. and known to many readers of "The Electrical Age" as Sophie Norvick, who is now settled in Winnipeg

FOR the past eight years, we in Canada have thought con- stantly of the people at home in Britain, and even when our rationing was most stringent and so many everyday needs could not be filled, our sympathies went out to the British housewife, who had still less food and many more difficulties to contend with. During my visit to Great Britain this summer I have been amazed at the achievements of the home-maker in counteract- ing that sameness in the taste and appearance of the dishes made from the meagre rations and limited variety of foodstuffs.
